title: (Coding) Write a Spring Kafka producer that publishes JSON events keyed by `userId`, a `@KafkaListener` consumer with MANUAL acknowledgment + bounded retries + DLT, and a batch-mode listener — and show pausing the listener when a downstream (DB) is unavailable and resuming on recovery.
shortTitle: (Coding) Write a Spring Kafka JSON producer, a manual-ack consumer with bounded retries and DLT, a batch listener, and listener pause/resume on downstream failure.

s1_definition.profdef: This coding task combines several Spring Kafka features into one cohesive service. A producer serializes events to JSON and publishes them keyed by userId so all of one user's events share a partition and stay ordered. A consumer uses manual acknowledgment so it commits the offset only after processing succeeds, with bounded retries and a dead letter topic for records that exhaust their attempts. A batch-mode listener processes a whole poll batch at once for throughput. Finally the service pauses its listener when a downstream database is unavailable and resumes when it recovers, so it never loses events or hammers a dead dependency.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India this is the full mailroom put together. The producer addresses each letter by the customer's id so all of Rajesh's letters go to one sorter and stay in order. The consumer only moves the bookmark after it has genuinely filed the letter, tries a few times if filing hiccups, and drops hopeless letters in the problem tray. The batch sorter grabs a whole tray at once for speed. And when the filing room, the database, is closed, the supervisor tells the sorter to pause so letters wait safely, and to resume when the room reopens.
s1_definition.oneliner: Produce JSON keyed by userId for ordering, consume with manual ack plus bounded retries plus a dead letter topic for safety, use a batch listener for throughput, and pause or resume the listener on downstream health.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This coding task combines several Spring Kafka features into one cohesive service. A producer serializes events to JSON and publishes them keyed by userId so all of one user's events share a partition and stay ordered. A consumer uses manual acknowledgment so it commits the offset only after processing succeeds, with bounded retries and a dead letter topic for records that exhaust their attempts. A batch-mode listener processes a whole poll batch at once for throughput. Finally the service pauses its listener when a downstream database is unavailable and resumes when it recovers, so it never loses events or hammers a dead dependency.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India this is the full mailroom put together. The producer addresses each letter by the customer's id so all of Rajesh's letters go to one sorter and stay in order. The consumer only moves the bookmark after it has genuinely filed the letter, tries a few times if filing hiccups, and drops hopeless letters in the problem tray. The batch sorter grabs a whole tray at once for speed. And when the filing room, the database, is closed, the supervisor tells the sorter to pause so letters wait safely, and to resume when the room reopens.

**One line to remember:** Produce JSON keyed by userId for ordering, consume with manual ack plus bounded retries plus a dead letter topic for safety, use a batch listener for throughput, and pause or resume the listener on downstream health.

sections.s2_technical:
The producer uses a JSON serializer so the value is written as JSON bytes, and it passes the userId as the key: `kafkaTemplate.send("user.events", userId, event)`. Keying by userId means Kafka hashes the key to pick a partition, so every event for the same user lands on the same partition and is therefore consumed in order. The send returns a CompletableFuture so you can log success with the resulting partition and offset or log a failure, without blocking.

The single-record consumer is configured with manual acknowledgment, so the container does not auto-commit; instead you inject an Acknowledgment and call acknowledge only after the work is done. You wrap the processing with bounded retries: if the business step throws a transient error you retry a fixed number of times with a backoff, and if it still fails or the error is permanent you forward the record to a dead letter topic and acknowledge so the main partition moves on. The important property is at-least-once, because you acknowledge only after success, so a crash before acknowledging causes a safe redelivery, and your processing stays idempotent to tolerate it.

The batch-mode listener is a different container configured to hand your method the whole list of records from one poll, for example `public void onBatch(List<UserEvent> events, Acknowledgment ack)`. You process the list, which is more efficient because you can do one bulk database write for many events, and then acknowledge once for the batch. Batch mode trades a slightly larger redelivery window, since a failure can replay the earlier records of the batch, for higher throughput, so you use it where per-record commit overhead matters and bulk operations are natural.

Pause and resume give runtime flow control tied to downstream health. You give the listener an id, inject the KafkaListenerEndpointRegistry, and when a health check detects the database is down you call pause on the container; the consumer stays in the group and keeps its partitions and heartbeats, so there is no rebalance, but it stops delivering records. When the database recovers you call resume and it continues from the last committed offset with nothing lost. The senior nuances are that keying by userId is what preserves ordering and also concentrates a hot user on one partition, which you mitigate with salting if needed; that manual acknowledgment must always acknowledge on both the success and the dead-letter paths or the partition stalls; that batch mode needs careful partial-failure handling because one bad record should not fail the whole batch, which you often handle by filtering the bad record to the dead letter topic and processing the rest; and that pausing is far healthier than letting the listener fail repeatedly against a dead database.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that a single user-activity service must publish events, consume them safely, process them in bulk for efficiency, and survive database outages without losing anything.

Problem 1 — events for a user must be processed in order, so a login must be seen before the transfer that follows it. This is exactly what keying by userId solves: all of Rajesh's events share a partition and stay ordered.

Problem 2 — the consumer must never lose an event and must isolate poison records. This is exactly what manual acknowledgment with bounded retries and a dead letter topic solves: acknowledge only after success, retry transient failures, and park hopeless records.

Problem 3 — at peak the per-record commit overhead is too high, and many events can be written to the database in one bulk statement. This is exactly what a batch listener solves.

Problem 4 — during database maintenance the consumer must stop cleanly and resume afterwards. This is exactly what pause and resume solves.

The code will define a UserEvent, a `UserEventPublisher` keyed by userId, a `UserEventConsumer` with manual ack, bounded retries, and dead letter routing, a `BatchUserEventConsumer` that bulk-processes a list, a `DatabaseHealth` flag, and a `ListenerControl` that pauses and resumes. The demo step is: publish several events for Rajesh and Priya, consume one with a transient failure that recovers and one poison record that goes to the dead letter topic, process a batch in bulk, then take the database down to pause and bring it back to resume.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway migration)
CREATE TABLE user_events (
    event_id  VARCHAR(40) PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    type      VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    detail    VARCHAR(200),
    stored_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE user_events_dlt (
    id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    event_id   VARCHAR(40),
    reason     VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    failed_at  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
      acks: all
    consumer:
      group-id: user-activity
      enable-auto-commit: false
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.json.trusted.packages: com.bank.activity.model
    listener:
      ack-mode: MANUAL_IMMEDIATE
bank:
  retry:
    max-attempts: 3
    backoff-ms: 500
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is several user-activity events for Rajesh and Priya, plus one poison record, flowing through all four features.

Step 1: The producer publishes E1, E2, and E3 as JSON keyed by userId. Rajesh's E1 and E2 hash to the same partition, so his login and transfer stay in order, and Priya's E3 goes to her partition.

Step 2: The manual-ack consumer processes E2. On the first attempt it throws a transient blip, so it retries after a backoff, succeeds on the second attempt, stores the event, and only then acknowledges, giving at-least-once safety.

Step 3: The consumer processes the poison record E9 of type CORRUPT. Processing throws a permanent error, so it is routed straight to the dead letter topic and acknowledged, keeping the partition flowing.

Step 4: The batch listener receives a batch of two events, E4 and E5, and writes them in one bulk database operation, then acknowledges the whole batch once, which is more efficient than per-record commits.

Step 5: The database goes down and the health check pauses the listener. Event E6 arrives but is held, offsets frozen, with no rebalance.

Step 6: The database recovers, the listener resumes, and E6 is drained and processed in order. The final state shows the stored events, one dead letter, and nothing lost.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Producer: send("user.events", userId, UserEvent)  (JSON, key=userId)
    │ hash(userId) % 4 → same user, same partition, ordered
    ▼
  Kafka: user.events (4 partitions)
    │
    ├─ single-record consumer (MANUAL_IMMEDIATE)
    │     process → ok? → ack
    │             → transient? → retry ×3 (backoff) → ok → ack
    │             → permanent/exhausted? → user.events.DLT → ack
    │
    ├─ batch listener (setBatchListener=true)
    │     List<UserEvent> → one bulk DB write → ack whole batch
    │
    └─ pause/resume control
          DB down → container.pause() (offsets frozen, no rebalance) → hold E6
          DB up   → container.resume() → drain E6 in order
```

     records flow          hold events        drain in order

sections.s6_takeaway:
This is the question where I show that I can wire the whole Spring Kafka toolkit into one coherent service. On the producing side I publish events as JSON keyed by the userId, because keying by userId makes Kafka route every event for one user to the same partition, which preserves per-user ordering, so a login is always consumed before the transfer that follows it, and the send returns a future I use to log the resulting partition or a failure.

On the consuming side I use manual acknowledgment, so I disable auto-commit and call acknowledge only after the processing succeeds, which gives at-least-once delivery. Around the processing I put bounded retries with a backoff for transient failures, and if the retries are exhausted or the error is permanent I route the record to a dead letter topic and still acknowledge, so the partition is never blocked by a poison record. Because delivery is at-least-once, I keep the processing idempotent so a redelivery is harmless.

I add a batch-mode listener for throughput, configured so the method receives the whole poll batch as a list, which lets me do one bulk database write for many events and acknowledge the batch once, trading a slightly larger replay window for much less commit overhead. And I wire pause and resume for downstream health: I give the listener an id, look it up through the endpoint registry, and when a health check sees the database is down I pause the container, which freezes the offsets and holds the consumer in the group without a rebalance, then resume when the database recovers so it continues exactly where it left off.

In the user-activity service at National Bank of India this exact design handled a transient database blip on Rajesh's transfer event with a quick retry, parked a corrupt event in the dead letter topic without stalling, bulk-inserted a batch efficiently, and sailed through a database maintenance window by pausing and resuming with nothing lost. The senior nuances I call out are that keying by userId can create a hot partition for a very active user, which I would mitigate with salting; that the manual-ack path must acknowledge on both the success and the dead-letter branches or the partition stalls; that batch mode needs partial-failure handling so one bad record in a batch is filtered to the dead letter topic rather than failing the whole batch; and that pausing is always healthier than letting a listener fail repeatedly against a dead dependency.

---

keyPoints: Dead Letter Topic (DLT): store failed messages for later analysis
Retry topic: automatic retry with backoff before DLT
Poison pill: message that always fails — skip or DLT
